title: AI-assisted deep learning segmentation and quantitative analysis of X-ray microtomography data
author: Strandberg, Chevreau, et al.

steps.title: Acquire X‑ray microtomography data
steps.instruction: Perform scans at the ANATOMIX beamline (Synchrotron SOLEIL) using a polychromatic white X‑ray beam (central photon energy ≈ 40 keV, electron beam current 100 mA). Record images with an ORCA Flash 4.0 V2 camera equipped with a 2× magnification lens, setting exposure between 10 ms and 50 ms per image. Use a field of view of 6.5 mm and a pixel resolution of 3.07 µm. Collect 1 600–5 900 projections while rotating the sample over a 180–360° range; apply extended‑field tomography for samples larger than the field of view.

steps.title: Reconstruct tomographic volumes
steps.instruction: Use the PyHST2 reconstruction software (filtered back‑projection algorithm) to reconstruct the raw projections. Apply a double flat‑field algorithm to reduce ring artefacts and employ a Paganini filter for semi‑quantitative phase retrieval.

steps.title: Prepare software environment
steps.instruction: Install Dragonfly (Version 2022.2, Windows, free academic license). Ensure the workstation has an Nvidia RTX A5000 GPU (24 GB VRAM) and 384 GB RAM.

steps.title: Segment images and create training data
steps.instruction: Within Dragonfly, launch the Segmentation Wizard to label tomographic images, build a database, and generate training and validation datasets for the deep‑learning model. All models are built using Dragonfly’s native toolkits.

steps.title: Train deep‑learning model
steps.instruction: Train the model using the ORS categorical cross‑entropy loss function. Stop training after 27 epochs because validation loss did not improve for 15 consecutive epochs. Record training loss = 0.0042, validation loss = 0.0017, ORS dice coefficient = 0.997, and validation dice coefficient = 0.998.

steps.title: Validate model on ash samples
steps.instruction: Apply the trained model to additional ash samples. Compute segmentation scores, which range from 0.9987 to 0.9994 across all tested samples. When scanning replicate samples with identical settings, reuse the existing model; retrain only if material or acquisition settings change.

steps.title: Post‑process segmentation
steps.instruction: Perform morphological operations: apply the “Close” operation followed by “Fill inner areas” to obtain consistent identification of open pores versus background.

steps.title: Quantitative analysis and comparison
steps.instruction: Calculate porosity, open‑pore volume, mean equivalent pore diameter, average wall thickness, and specific surface area for each sample. Compare results with the reference method (Strandberg et al.). For Sample 1: Porosity 13.1 % (new) vs 12.5 % (ref); Open pore volume 15.1 % vs 20.0 %; Mean equivalent diameter 16.2 µm vs 18.5 µm; Wall thickness 8.6 µm vs 7.7 µm; Specific surface area 10.0 mm² mm⁻³ vs 10.5 mm² mm⁻³. For Sample 2: Porosity 16.8 % vs 14.9 %; Open pore volume 38.9 % vs 50.6 %; Mean equivalent diameter 15.6 µm vs 15.0 µm; Wall thickness 4.6 µm vs 4.1 µm; Specific surface area 0.87 mm² mm⁻³ vs 0.61 mm² mm⁻³. Note that the new method uses a volume‑thickness map, whereas the reference method uses Avizo 9.3 with a Chamfer Distance Map.

description: To validate the deep learning model, the loss function ORS categorical cross-entropy was used. The ORS dice coefficient and the validation ORS dice coefficient was 0.997 respective 0.998 after 27 epochs, 1 being the maximum. The training was stopped after 27 epochs, due to no improvement in the validation loss in 15 consecutives epochs. In Fig. 7 the results of the training and validation losses can be seen, the training and validation loss are 0.0042 and 0.0017 after 27 epochs, respectively. A lower value is favourable, indicating a good accuracy of the model for prediction.Fig. 7Loss and validation loss during training as a function of epochs.Fig. 7 For further validation the method was applied to other ash samples. The method's segmentation part is validated. Comparing the segmented data to the training data gave scores between 0.9987 and 0.9994 for all tested samples, which shows the share of pixels predicted correctly. The method works well for single ash particles. When tested on replicates of the same material, scanned with the same settings, the previously trained deep learning model could be applied without additional training with an acceptable result. However, results improved when a model trained explicitly for the new sample was used. It's important to note that training a new model becomes necessary when the material or settings are altered. Due to the highly irregular shapes of the ash particles, assessing what constitutes open pores and the boundary to the background is a matter of judgment, and it is difficult to quantitatively validate its accuracy. However, the morphological operation “Close” and the operation “Fill inner areas” give the same results with repeated tests. To better validate what is open pores versus background further studies is needed, especially for other types of samples.
